## §195 · The traversal finished — and the one requirement that was rendered in the wrong place to be found

### §195.1 · Ecosystem's "plans" was built, and unlocatable

Ecosystem's stated requirement is *"monetisation (**plans**, payouts, commission)"*. The
payout split and the commission decomposition are on its card; the **plan** figures are the
**per-stream breakdown** migration 178 publishes — and `AdminMetricsPanel` renders them on the
**Control Center**, under the Dashboard's own *"revenue by stream"* requirement.

So nothing was missing, and nothing was duplicated — but an operator on Ecosystem looking for
per-plan revenue had **no way to know it existed**, and §184's audit of that page had not
recorded it either way. The card now says where the figures are. Duplicating it would have
shown one set of numbers in two places with no ruling that it belongs in both; the design's own
interaction model cross-links instead, which is the pattern the Dashboard's audit-tail line
also follows.

### §195.2 · Every page's requirement list, reconciled

| page | requirements | built | stated absent | unlocated until now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Control Center | 12 | 5 | **7 (§194)** | — |
| Ecosystem | 5 | 4 | 1 | **1 (plans → Dashboard)** |
| People | 4 | 2 | **3 → 4 (§193)** | — |
| Trust | 4 | 3 | 1 | — |
| Operations | 3 | 3 | — | — |
| Settings | 12 sections | 5 | **7 (prose said 6, §193.2a)** | — |

**Three of the six censuses miscounted what they were describing**, and in three different
ways: People's audit named three absences where the list had four (the figure was genuinely
unbuilt); Settings' prose named six where its own test said seven (the code was already
right); and the Control Center stated none at all. Each was found by **re-running the
measurement against the published list** rather than re-reading the conclusion — which is the
§181 method, and it is now the third time it has paid.

### §195.3 · Owner pack — fourth revision

`Q6` closed by existing authority. `Q8`, `Q9`, `Q10` answered and discharged in §191, with the
rulings recorded verbatim and what each changed stated beside it — including that **Q8 and Q10
changed no behaviour**, so "no change needed" was the correct answer and is recorded as such.

Two new questions, and both came from re-running a measurement rather than from new work:

* **`Q11` · What is churn?** The one Control Center requirement with **no ruling at all** — it
  is absent from the decision sheet's twelve IDs, so it was never asked. A definition needs
  the denominator population, the window, and what event constitutes leaving. Not inventable:
  `COWORK` §8 forbids agents inventing monetisation.
* **`Q12` · Is a Control Center audit tail wanted, or is the Trust deep-link the answer?**
  `admin_audit_events` already backs it, so this is **buildable today** — but
  `SCREEN-INVENTORY` also states that *"every 'View audit history' link deep-links to
  Trust > Audit logs"*. The two statements point different ways, and duplicating a projection
  is a placement decision rather than a mechanical one.

## §197 · Owner decisions Q11 and Q12, implemented — and a question I had raised in error

### §197.1 · Q11 · the data contract, and what it refuses to compute

**The ruling:** *"Option B — Subscription churn, event-based … subscriptions canceled during
the month ÷ active subscriptions at the beginning of the month."* Recorded as **`METRIC-20`**
on the decision sheet, where churn had never appeared.

**Migration 180 adds one nullable column and backfills nothing.** `subscriptions.canceled_at`
arrives empty across all 173 pre-existing rows, and that null is the truthful answer: every one
is `status = 'active'`, so none has a cancellation date, and for any that later did there is no
authoritative source for *when*. Deriving one from `updated_at` or `current_period_end` is
exactly the inference the ruling forbids — one moves on any write, the other is a billing
boundary rather than a departure.

**The authorized writer is the one that already existed.** No trigger and no new RPC:
`stripe-webhook` already handles `customer.subscription.deleted` and already writes
`status = 'canceled'` there, so the timestamp is written in the **same update**, taking
**Stripe's own `canceled_at`** and naming its fallback rather than hiding it. A trigger
inferring `now()` from a status transition would record when *we noticed*, and would fire for
repairs and backfills too.

**Spelling, deliberately inconsistent.** `canceled_at`, one L, matching Stripe's field and this
table's own `'canceled'` status value. `coach_client_relationships.cancelled_at` has two. The
divergence is pre-existing and was **not renamed** — a rename is a contract change to a column
172 and 179 already read.

**The denominator, and the one imprecision it cannot avoid.** "Active at the beginning of the
month" is computed from the two authoritative timestamps only: `created_at` before the month
began, and not yet canceled then. **It does not consult `status`**, because `status` is a
current value with no history and applying it to a past instant would assert that a row which
is `past_due` today was `past_due` a month ago. A subscription that never activated is
therefore counted. That is disclosed *on the surface* — `churn_denominator_basis` is a view
column, so the card states the basis rather than a reader having to infer it.

**Insufficient history is not 0%.** `churn_rate_pct` is **NULL until any cancellation has ever
been recorded**, because before that the measure cannot distinguish *"nobody left"* from *"we
were not recording departures"*. After the first recorded cancellation the mechanism is proven
live and a month with none is a **real** zero. `churn_first_cancellation_at` publishes how much
history exists, as a fact.

`Q1` and `Q2` cannot reach this: the population is **subscriptions** and the month boundary is
the database's, the same basis 172/176/179 use. **No plan-level split**, because `Q13` is
unresolved — and D20 asserts no `churn_*` column carries a plan, kind or tier.

### §197.2 · Q12 · the tail, built to the width of the ruling

**The ruling:** *"Option A — actor-anonymous audit tail"*, displaying action, category,
outcome, timestamp and required disclosure, and **not** resolving actor IDs into names.

`_RecentAdminActivity` reads the existing `admin_audit_events` — no new surface, no new grant,
no schema. Four things are absent, each a different kind of absence:

* **No actor name.** The projection carries `actor_id` as a raw uuid and this widget never
  reads it. D20 §6 goes further and proves the **surface itself** exposes no name or email
  column at all, so the constraint is structural rather than a widget convention.
* **No Guardian rows.** `agent_action` is a real category in the 15-value CHECK and **nothing
  emits it** (`B-17` / `P7`).
* **No release rows.** *"Release 4.2.0 deployed to staging"* is **not an audit event** under the
  ruled vocabulary; release state lives in `release_status` (173) and is already on this page's
  QA & release card.
* **No MFA.** The sample row claims a second factor that is not a recorded fact.

**`A13·1` is disclosed, not implied.** The projection excludes the reader's own `admin_action`
rows in its own predicate, so the tail is **incomplete for whoever is reading it** — and a
ledger that looks complete while excluding its reader is worse than one that says so.

**The "Not shown here" card dropped from seven absences to six**, and the guard's expected count
came down with it. That is an absence becoming a **build**, not a relaxed guard: its substance —
distinct reasons, each naming a ruling or a missing producer, none reading as a measured zero —
is unchanged, and a new assertion requires that `Audit-log tail` is **no longer** in the map.

### §197.3 · Q13 — evidence gathered, nothing patched

`subscriptions.kind` is `'app'` on all 173 QA rows while `022:17-19` documents
`'coach' | 'self_guided' | 'ai_guided'`, and there is no CHECK. Two facts narrow it
considerably, and neither decides it:

1. **Every `'app'` row has a null `stripe_subscription_id` and a null `stripe_price_id`.** They
   did not arrive through Stripe.
2. **No code anywhere writes `kind = 'app'`.** `create-checkout` and `stripe-webhook` write the
   documented vocabulary and always set the Stripe identifiers.

So the `'app'` rows are **seed data, not subscriptions any code path produced**. That is
evidence that the comment is the live contract and the data is QA noise — and it is still the
owner's call, because the alternative (that `'app'` is an intended value this repo does not yet
write) cannot be excluded from inside the repo. **No CHECK was added, no vocabulary changed, no
row touched.**

### §197.4 · Q14 — I raised this in error, and the correction matters more than the question

I reported to the owner that *"one cancelled relationship has no `cancelled_at`"*. **That was a
measurement taken while one of my own test fixtures was live.** `D01` flips a relationship to
`cancelled` as part of its run — and at `d01:217` and `:232` it sets `cancelled_at` explicitly.

Measured with no suite running: **176 relationships, every one `active`, `cancelled_at`
populated on zero rows.** There is no cancelled relationship in QA at all, so the null column is
an **empty population** and not a writer gap. And there is no writer gap: **three production
paths** set `cancelled_at` in the same write as the status —
`coach_relationship_service.dart:104`, `profile_screen.dart:918` and
`intake_flow_screen.dart:4188`.

**So Q14's premise is withdrawn.** It is kept visible rather than deleted, because a question
put to an owner on a bad measurement should be corrected where it was asked. If a `NOT NULL` or
a trigger is still wanted it is a **policy** choice, and there is no observed defect motivating
one.

**The lesson is the run's own, repeated.** Every earlier instance was a measurement that read
its own notes; this one read its own fixtures. The reading was taken mid-suite, and the fix is
the same discipline that caught the others: measure when nothing else is writing, and say which
it was.

### §197.5 · Evidence

**D20 · 23/23 live** — the decisive pair (numerator `0` while the rate is `NULL`), the
transition to a **real** `0` once a prior-month cancellation exists, a numerator delta of
exactly one, the rate recomputed independently from the view's own published components, the
no-backfill proof across 175 rows, no plan/kind/tier among the `churn_*` columns, no uuid or
email disclosed, and an **asserted** teardown — `subscriptions` is a billing table and a stray
row would misstate revenue on surfaces other suites read.

**Four defects in that suite were mine, each caught by an assertion rather than a green run:**
`/plan/` matched `stream_coach_plan_cents` — 178's revenue-by-stream column, a true regex match
and a false claim, so the check is now scoped to `churn_*`; the denial case used `support`,
which **holds** `Monetization·view` — all five approved roles do (`155:49-53`), so the only
denial the matrix makes reachable is a caller with **no admin role**; and the audit projection
was read through `svc`, where `admin_can` is false for `service_role`, which reported the gate
working as a missing projection.

Live **1074/1074 across 20 suites** (1051/19 before D20) · Flutter **1917 / 5 skipped**
(1907 → 1917) · `dart analyze` **0 errors** · nine static guards exit 0 · QA frontier
**179 → 180**, declared and reconciled.

**Production was not contacted.**

## §198 · The interaction model — the one design list never traversed

### §198.1 · The method, applied to a list I had not read as requirements

§181's method is to traverse the published design's own lists rather than the programme's
notes about them. It had been applied three times to *"Data each page needs"*. **It had never
been applied to `SCREEN-INVENTORY`'s "Interactions expected"**, which is a requirements list in
the same document, one heading above:

> *"Attention queue opens a drawer; every "View audit history" link deep-links to Trust >
> Audit logs; before/after diffs deep-link to a Trust audit event; Settings links across to
> Operations > System events, Trust > Authorization and Trust > AI Guardian; global search and
> filters on tables; row actions open confirm dialogs for destructive changes."*

Six requirements. Traversed:

| requirement | state |
|---|---|
| Attention queue opens a drawer | **built in substance.** The drawer is the queue's container — a transform/scrim animation in the desktop mock — and the queue itself renders severity, summary, scope and the `Investigate` disclosure. The chrome is a layout choice; the content is the requirement. |
| every *"View audit history"* link deep-links to Trust > Audit logs | **WAS MISSING — now built** (§198.2) |
| before/after diffs deep-link to a Trust audit event | **moot by owner decision**, and now stated (§198.3) |
| Settings links across to Operations > System events, Trust > Authorization, Trust > AI Guardian | **WAS MISSING — now built** (§198.2) |
| global search and filters on tables | **not built**, and recorded with its reason (§198.4) |
| row actions open confirm dialogs for destructive changes | **built** — moderation hide/dismiss, the Guardian disable, incident resolve |

### §198.2 · Ten links the page did not have

The approved Settings screen carries **ten** `View audit history →` links — one per section —
plus six named cross-links: `Trust → Authorization`, `Trust → AI Guardian`,
`Trust → Audit logs`, `Trust → Security`, `Operations → System events` and
`Operations → Integrations`. **The built page had none**, so an operator reading a Settings
section had no route to the record of what changed it.

`AdminCrossLink` and a `sectionLinks` map now carry them, and three properties are asserted
rather than assumed: every label is **the design's own** (trailing arrow included — a
paraphrase would not match the screen it implements), every destination is a **built admin
route**, and a section the design gives no link **gets none**. Two tests drive a **real
`GoRouter`** and tap through, so the destinations are proved by arriving rather than by reading
the route string back out of the widget.

**The links sit outside each card's `when`**, so the route to the record exists in every
state — including the one where the figure itself could not be read. And **unbacked sections
get them too**: what changed a setting is logged whether or not the setting is stored.

The page remains **read-only**, and its read-only assertion still passes — a navigation link is
not a write.

### §198.3 · "before/after" is absent by ruling, and Trust now says so

Trust's own stated requirement is *"immutable audit log with **before/after**"*, and the
before/after half is absent by **owner decision B-19 — "withhold both"** `delta` and
`changed_columns` in the Admin audit projections, *"closes as a CONFIRMED DESIGN. The
projections stay exactly as shipped."* The columns exist — 150 added them for `A6` delta
capture — and 156/159 deliberately do not project them.

So the interaction requirement is **moot**: there are no diffs in this layer to deep-link to.
But the audit card stated `A13·1` and **not** this, which is the §194 pattern one page over — a
requirement half that is absent by ruling, with no sentence saying why. It says so now, and a
test requires both that the sentence is present and that **nothing reconstructs a diff** from
what is projected.

### §198.4 · Search and filters — recorded, not built

Not built, and the reason is split:

* **The filter vocabularies are partly unknown and partly unbacked.** The approved tables show
  `Status: All`, `Type: All`, `Host: Any`, `Visibility: All`, `Verification: All`,
  `Specialism: All`, `Difficulty: Any`, `Duration: Any`, `Renews: Any` — closed selects, so the
  option lists are not visible. Several key columns do not exist at all: event **type** has no
  column (§193), program **status** has no lifecycle (§193), **verification** has no state
  (§185.2), and **visibility** has no column. A filter over a column that does not exist cannot
  be built, and one whose options are invisible would have to invent them.
* **Search is backed but would be a false affordance as the lists stand.** `Search name or
  email` names its own fields, and the data is already read — but every admin list is rendered
  with a `take(10)`/`take(20)` cap, so a client-side search would search a ten-row window and
  report "no match" for records that exist. Doing it honestly means **server-side filtering**:
  new query parameters on each read, and a live assertion per surface that the filter narrows
  rather than silently empties. That is real work rather than a boundary, and it is recorded
  here as the next reachable item rather than half-built.

## §199 · Search — built server-side, with the fields it searched stated

### §199.1 · Why it had to be server-side, and why that was the whole difficulty

§198.4 recorded search as *"backed but a false affordance as the lists stand"*: every admin
list renders a `take(10)`/`take(20)` page, so filtering what is already on screen searches a
twenty-row window and answers *"no match"* for records that exist. **A false negative dressed
as an answer** is worse than no search box.

So the query goes to the query. `getUserDirectory` and `eventDirectory` take an optional
`query`, build the filter in PostgREST, and the providers re-run the read when the box changes.
D21 proves the filter **narrows** against a 945-row population rather than emptying.

### §199.2 · The two placeholders do not promise the same thing, and the UI says so

* **People** — *"Search name or email"*. The approved placeholder **names its fields**, so the
  filter is `first_name` / `last_name` / `email` by the design's own words.
* **Events** — *"Search events"*. It names nothing. The title is the minimal faithful reading;
  adding location or host would be choosing scope the design did not specify. So the card
  states *"Searches the event title only. Location, host and status are not matched"* — and
  D21 proves that claim by giving a fixture event a **distinct marker in its location** and
  requiring a location search to find **nothing**.

**A zero result is worded by its cause.** With no query, People says *"None"* and Events says
the approved *"No events in this range."*; with a query active they say *"No account matches
that search"* and *"No event title matches that search"*. Rendering one sentence for both would
make a filter look like a fact about the population — the same error class as a null rate
rendering as `0%`.

### §199.3 · The sanitiser is a security control, not tidying

PostgREST's filter grammar **is punctuation**: `or=(a.ilike.*x*,b.ilike.*x*)` parses on
`,` `.` `(` `)` `*`. A query containing those does not merely fail to match — it **re-parses
the expression**, and on an `or=` that is a **widening**: a crafted value can append a disjunct
and make the filter match rows the operator never asked for. These surfaces are gated by
`admin_can`, so it is not a privilege escape; it is still a query the operator did not write.

`_searchTerm` **strips** the grammar characters rather than escaping them, because PostgREST's
quoting rules differ per operator and version — an escape that is correct today is a dependency
on a parser detail, while removing the characters cannot be wrong. `%` and `_` go too: they are
LIKE wildcards, and leaving them would let a typed `%` silently widen the match.

D21 §3 sends the four payloads the service would have sent without the strip, and the decisive
property is **not** that they fail. One of them — `x*)` — **parses and returns 200 with one
row**, which is narrower than the population and therefore harmless. The assertion is that no
crafted query ever returns **more** than the unfiltered population, which is what "cannot
widen" actually means.

And §4 proves a filter is not a route around the gate: an unauthorized caller gets **zero rows
from the same well-formed filter that returned the row a moment earlier** — so it is the gate
refusing, not a malformed request failing.

### §199.4 · Four harness defects, and one that would have inverted the conclusion

The first run reported `matched=0 of 945` and I nearly recorded "the filter does not work".
**It had never been evaluated.** A raw `%` in a URL begins an escape sequence, so
`ilike.%QA%` is malformed and PostgREST answers 500 — which the suite was reading as an empty
result set. The shipped Dart service does **not** have this bug: `postgrest-2.7.1` builds
filters through `appendSearchParams` → `Uri.replace(queryParameters:)`, which percent-encodes
every value. The harness now encodes `%` as `%25` and **leaves the grammar characters raw**, or
§3's payloads could not attempt the re-parse they exist to attempt.

Three more, each caught by an assertion:

* `countExact` supplied the widening baseline through **service_role**, for which `admin_can`
  is false — so `population=0` and the comparison was vacuous. The same mistake D20 §6 made
  against the audit projection, now with a non-vacuity check beside it.
* A widget assertion claimed the placeholder must not be findable as text. **It is** — Flutter
  renders a hint as a `Text` descendant of the field, so `widgetWithText` matches. The claim
  was about the **controller**, which is what it reads now.
* One test pumped a second tree over the first to compare two states; that is not a fresh
  mount, and the second assertion read the first tree's state. Split into two tests.

### §199.5 · What is still not built

**Filters** — the approved tables' `Status: All` / `Type: All` / `Verification: All` /
`Specialism: All` / `Visibility: All` / `Difficulty: Any` selects are **closed** in every
screenshot, so their option lists are not visible, and four of the columns behind them do not
exist at all: event **type** (§193), program **status** lifecycle (§193), coach
**verification** (§185.2) and event **visibility**. A filter over a column that does not exist
cannot be built and one whose options are invisible would have to invent them.

### §199.6 · Evidence

**D21 · 16/16 live** · live **1089/1089 across 21 suites** · Flutter **1932 / 5 skipped**
(1925 → 1932) · `dart analyze` **0 errors** · nine static guards exit 0. **No migration, no
schema change, no new grant** — the filters run inside the gates that already governed these
reads.

**Production was not contacted.**

## §200 · The third design list — the state system, documented on two pages of six

### §200.1 · "States designed" is a requirements list too

`SCREEN-INVENTORY` carries **three** requirements lists, not two. §181's method found work in
*"Data each page needs"* three times and §198 found two missing requirements in *"Interactions
expected"*. **"States designed"** had never been read as requirements at all:

> *"Loading, Empty, Error, Permission (denied), Degraded. Also: Unavailable (Control Center,
> Operations, People), Stale (People, Trust), Offline and Skeleton (Ecosystem, People),
> Read-only (Operations, Settings, Trust). A "State system" panel on People, Trust, Operations
> and Settings and "Dashboard states" on the Control Center show the patterns side by side."*

Two findings:

1. **Two of the five required panels were missing.** The design places a `State system` panel
   on **four** pages and `Dashboard states` on the Control Center. **Operations had none**, and
   the **Control Center had none** — and the Control Center's label is a different one, which
   the inventory states separately.
2. **Four of the ten designed states are implemented nowhere**, and before this section each
   panel listed only the states its own page happened to render — so **Offline, Stale, Degraded
   and Skeleton were silently absent on all six surfaces.** That is §194's defect one level up:
   not a missing figure, a missing *state vocabulary*.

### §200.2 · Why those four are not built, stated once

Each needs a definition, and inventing one would put a state on screen that no rule produces:

* **Offline** — no connectivity signal exists in this layer.
* **Stale** — *how old is stale?* is a product rule, not a default.
* **Degraded** — needs a definition of partial failure. **`A5` uses the same word for the
  Guardian's own recorded state**, which is a different thing entirely: that is a value in a
  column, not a condition of a page. Conflating them would have been the easiest mistake here.
* **Skeleton** — a loading *treatment*; this layer renders Loading as text, and a shimmer would
  say nothing the text does not.

`AdminStatesPanel` holds them in **one constant**, and `SEC-G10` requires every panel to route
through it — because six hand-written lists diverge the first time one page changes, and a
divergence here is a page claiming a state it does not have.

### §200.3 · A shared sentence that misdescribed a page

The first version of the shared panel used **one** read-only line for all five pages — *"This
page is read-only except where an action is shown"* — and the Settings test failed. It was
right to: **Settings has no actions at all**, so that sentence made it claim one.

The posture is now per-page and the guard requires all five to **differ**: Settings and
Operations are read-only outright; People names *"Edit profile"*; Trust names the incident
resolve and Guardian disable; the Control Center says every action lives on the page that owns
the record. A panel whose job is to document the state system must not misdescribe the page it
sits on.

### §200.4 · Evidence

`SEC-G10` · **5 assertions**, including a control that proves the hand-rolled-list detector
works and a distinctness check on the five postures. Admin screen suites **115** · Flutter
**1937 / 5 skipped** (1932 → 1937) · `dart analyze` **0 errors**. **No migration, no schema, no
new data read, no new grant.**

**Production was not contacted.**

## §201 · The component inventory, and the one item that is width-independent

### §201.1 · The fourth list, and the limit the design puts on it

`COMPONENTS.md` is the fourth requirements list. It names the shell (*"environment strip
(34px)"*, header with six-item nav, user menu, search), containers, data components (table with
sticky header, stat tile, **sparkline/bar/line chart**, severity badge, status pill, progress
bar, timeline, audit row with before/after diff), inputs (text, select, segmented control,
switch, checkbox, radio, search, **date range**) and feedback (toast, inline error, empty
state, skeleton, degraded banner, permission-denied panel, read-only banner).

**`RESPONSIVE.md` bounds what that list can require here, and the design says so itself:**

> *"A phone layout below 480px has **not** been separately designed for Admin (Admin is an
> operator tool); recorded as a gap."*

The whole document is *"designed for desktop first (1440 reference)"*, with navigation
collapsing *"to a compact bar"* only at 900px. So sticky-header tables, date ranges and the
six-item header nav are **desktop constructs with no approved sub-480px form** — and the design
records that as its own gap rather than leaving it to be inferred. `COMPONENTS.md` also records
that *"a separate per-component specification sheet (anatomy, variants, spacing annotations) has
**not** been produced."*

**Charts are a second kind of absence.** `sparkline/bar/line chart` would need a charting
dependency, which is a dependency decision of the same shape as `Q5`'s Phosphor icons — not
something to add while implementing a component list.

### §201.2 · The environment strip, which no width argument excuses

One item is width-independent, safety-bearing and fully specified: the **34px environment
strip**. The Control Center's own architectural-verification panel states the rule:

> *"No banner. Only staging and development show the amber strip at the top."*

**It was not built anywhere in the app.** And the production arm is the one a careless
implementation gets wrong in the *safe-looking* direction: a strip that appears in production is
a permanent false alarm operators learn to ignore, while one that fails to appear in staging lets
an operator act on what they believe is a sandbox. Both arms are asserted.

**Staging gets the design's verbatim sentence** — *"Staging environment — changes here do not
affect members"* — and it is **true in this repository** rather than merely copied: QA is a
separate Supabase project, which is the separation `ENV-5`'s production-ref guard exists to
enforce.

**Development deliberately does not get that sentence.** The design says development shows a
strip and **does not give its wording**, and the guarantee cannot be carried across: `ENV-4`
leaves `dev` with **no backend default**, so a development build points at whatever
`SUPABASE_URL` it was given. Promising that changes do not affect members would be a claim this
layer cannot make, so the dev strip names the environment and says where the backend came from.

Two smaller points, both asserted: the amber is the **generated token**
(`--adm-color-status-warning`) with the foreground token made *for* that fill
(`--adm-color-text-on-warning`) — using `colorStatusWarningText`, which is for warning text on
the page surface, would have been amber on amber. And the strip is read through a **provider**
rather than `AppEnv.current`, because that is a `static final` resolved once, so the prod arm —
the important one — could not otherwise be tested.

### §201.3 · Evidence

**7 assertions**, including the production arm (no text **and** zero preferred height, so it
cannot push the page down invisibly), the staging and dev arms, the 34px spec, the token pair,
a check that **all six** pages carry it, and one that exactly one `AppEnvironment` value maps to
no strip and that value is `prod`.

Widget suites **511 → 518** · Flutter **1944 / 5 skipped** (1937 → 1944) · `dart analyze`
**0 errors**. **No migration, no schema, no new data read, no new dependency.**

**Production was not contacted.**

| **E** | five existing V5 decisions | all four resolved (`METRIC-05`, `METRIC-06b`, `PD-A24`/`METRIC-16`, `METRIC-18`) **plus severity**, which is row A |
| **F** | implementation gaps | each built or recorded: admin data layer **built**; Guardian `B-17`/`P7`; service health no surface; CI feed `Q3`; wearable `PD-G01`; append-only audit store **exists** |
| **G** | `--adm-*` tokens vs Helix tiers | **OPEN · architecture — also MISSING from the pack.** Now `Q16` |

**Five of seven were already handled. Two were not in the pack at all**, and both were open in
the programme record the whole time — so this is an omission in my consolidated queue rather
than a new discovery, and it is recorded that way.

### §202.2 · `Q15` · the severity vocabulary, with nothing at risk today

The spec says `Critical · High · Warning · Informational`; the approved screens show
`CRITICAL · HIGH · MEDIUM · LOW`. The programme had already narrowed it three times (§12132):
the spec and the **shipped enum agree** — `143:70` enforces the spec's four with a CHECK —
`Risk` is a distinct axis, and **a fifth value, `"Severity set to Elevated"`, appears in
Trust**, so the design's own vocabulary is not internally settled.

**Nothing is at risk in the implementation**, which is worth stating because it changes the
decision's urgency rather than its substance: `_severityColor` and `_severityTint` map the three
coloured values and send everything else to neutral, *"rendered neutrally rather than guessed
into a danger colour"*. A `MEDIUM` arriving — which the CHECK currently forbids — would be
legible rather than mis-coloured.

### §202.3 · `Q16` · which Helix is canonical

Row G calls the token relationship an *"architecture question"*, and §103 had already found
something sharper than a question about tiers: **two artefacts both claim to be the 12Circle
Helix theme.**

* the **in-repo Dart implementation** — violet, Schibsted Grotesk, **conformance-tested in CI**;
* `/Users/dmac/Documents/projects/helix`'s `src/themes/12circle.ts` — **electric lime
  `#9EF01A`**, Hanken Grotesk / Clash Display, whose own header reads *"FIRST PASS — values are
  meant to be tuned by design."*

§103.1 separately established that **eleven of eleven shared colour roles match** between the
Admin tokens and the in-repo theme, along with the typeface, both hairline strengths and the
easing curve — *"one design system, not two that happen to agree."* So the `--adm-*` layer is a
**normalisation of the live theme**, not a rival to it, and row G's question is answered in that
direction.

What remains open is narrower and outside this repository: **which artefact a future product
binds to.** Nothing here depends on it; the enforced in-repo theme is live. §103.2's own words
are the reason it is not settled here: *"Which is canonical is a design-system authority
decision and is not made here."*

### §202.4 · Evidence

No code changed. The design-citation guard resolves every new reference (**exit 0**), and the
owner pack now carries **Q13 · Q15 · Q16** open, with `Q14`'s premise withdrawn and
`Q11`/`Q12` answered and implemented.

**Production was not contacted.**

## §203 · A page cap that broke one assertion loudly and another silently

### §203.1 · CI caught it, and it was not a regression from the change under test

The negative-control job's own fix went green, and the **Live QA** job failed on the same run
with a single assertion:

```
x admin_user_overview.users_total matches the real population — view=1005 actual=1000
```

**Nothing in that commit touched the database.** D15's baseline was
`svc('user_profiles?select=id&limit=1000')` and counted the **body length**, so the moment QA's
user population crossed **1000** the baseline saturated while the view stayed right. **The view
was never wrong; the measurement was.** This is the §187 lesson that produced `countExact` —
an equality against a page-capped count is correct only until the population reaches the cap.

### §203.2 · The silent one was worse

Fixing only the assertion that failed would have left the identical defect armed twice over.
Two more sites carried it:

* **`admin_events_overview.events_total`** — the same shape, **latent** rather than broken only
  because `events` is still under the cap.
* **The Users-directory equality** — `n(usersVia.body) === n(usersSvc.body)` with **both sides**
  capped at `limit=1000`. Once the population passed the cap it was comparing **1000 to 1000**:
  **green and meaningless.** It is the more dangerous sibling of the one that failed, because it
  would never have reported anything.

All three now use exact, header-derived counts.

### §203.3 · `countExactAs` — and why `countExact` could not be reused

`admin_user_directory` is gated on `admin_can('Users','view')`, which is **false for
`service_role`**, so a service-role count of it is **0** — replacing a blind assertion with a
vacuous one. `countExactAs(who, path)` counts the population the **caller** can see, and
refuses a missing content-range exactly as `countExact` does. D20 §6 and D21 §3 each made the
service-role mistake once; this is the instrument that removes the opportunity.

**The equality itself was verified before being asserted.** `160:37` projects
`FROM public.user_profiles` with **no row predicate** — the `WHERE admin_can(...)` is a gate,
not a filter — so a Viewer must see every profile. Measured at the time of the change:
**1005 = 1005**. An earlier reading of 945 in D21 was a different moment in QA's growth, not a
discrepancy.

### §203.4 · Evidence

D15 **353/353** · live **1089/1089 across 21 suites** · no schema, migration or policy touched
— three test baselines and one new library helper.

**Production was not contacted.**

## §204 · Q16 implemented in Helix — and the lime was never confined to source

### §204.1 · The owner resolved the authority question Option 3 had deferred

`Q16` closed as **Option 3 — preserve both**, which deferred the authority question rather than
answering it. The owner then superseded that: ***"12Circle is not using the lime theme. Violet is
the canonical 12Circle brand theme."*** The approved path became **Option 1a — retune the
registered Helix theme; do not delete it.**

Implemented in `akutonsol/helix-design-system`, branch `fix/12circle-violet-theme`, baseline
`ce7087a` → `309f291`, [PR #1](https://github.com/akutonsol/helix-design-system/pull/1).

The authorizing record is the owner's own commit `7de74d8`, which added **§29** to
`V5_OWNER_DECISION_PACK_CONSOLIDATED.md` and set the boundary this section answers to:
*"Implementation must occur in that source repository and be verified there; until then, `Q16` is
**decision-resolved, implementation-pending**."* It is now implementation-complete and verified.
That commit landed in parallel with this work and was **rebased onto, not over** — §29 and §204
are complementary, and §29's independent conclusion that *"`Q5` may be evaluated against the
authoritative violet design system"* corroborates §204.7 rather than resting on it.

### §204.2 · The risk was concrete, not theoretical

`dist/` is gitignored, which reads like containment. It is not: `package.json` runs
`prepare: npm run build`, so every **git-install consumer builds the themes on install**. The
baseline build at `ce7087a` emitted **13 lime bindings** into `dist/themes/12circle.css` —
`--color-accent`, `--color-accent-hover`, `--color-accent-subtle`, `--color-ring` in each of the
three blocks, plus the `--shadow-glow` halo. The superseded first pass was shipping.

### §204.3 · The retune was structural, not chromatic — and the shipped theme said so first

The decisive source was `apps/mobile/lib/core/theme/twelve_circle_theme.dart`, because it already
expresses 12 Circle **in Helix's own vocabulary** (`HelixSemantics`). Where
`admin.tokens.css @ 931218b` offers a five-step text ladder and this contract has three, the Dart
fixes the mapping — `textPrimary=ink, textSecondary=grey, textTertiary=dim` — so the three-step
answer is transcription, not my compression of a five-step one.

It also carries explicit `was:` annotations recording that it had **already rejected four of the
Helix theme's first-pass choices**:

| dimension | authoritative position | first pass in Helix |
|---|---|---|
| radius | *"cards 16, controls flat 12. **Explicitly NOT pill**"* | `full` / `2xl` — pill controls |
| motion | *"emphasised and brief. Nothing loops."* — `cubic-bezier(0.2,0,0,1)` / 200ms | `spring` overshoot / 220ms |
| type | *"one family throughout"* — Schibsted Grotesk | serif display + Hanken sans |
| shadow | *"no gradient, **no glow**"* | `0 0 24px rgba(158,240,26,.45)` neon halo |

**Aligning only the accent colour would have left the theme wrong in four other dimensions.** The
owner's instruction anticipated this — *"not just the accent color"* — and the evidence vindicated
it rather than merely permitting it.

One primitive did not fit: `HelixMotion.d200` is 200ms and this scale has no 200ms step
(`fast` 150 / `base` 220). `durationBrand` is authored as a literal. Substituting 220ms would have
been choosing the convenient value over the authoritative one.

### §204.4 · Two values the authority does not define — recorded, not invented

* **`accentHover` equals `accent`.** The system defines **exactly one** violet fill, `#7c3aed`,
  and no darker variant; a repo-wide search of the design authority returns a single violet. Hover
  is expressed as a **surface** change (`--adm-color-bg-hover: #1b1b20`), not a fill darkening.
  `#a78bfa` is the accent-**text** colour — `a:hover` pairs it with `#c4b1fc` for links, and white
  on it is **2.72:1**, which fails AA outright. So equality here *records the authority's actual
  position*: the fill does not move. Inventing a darker violet would have been inventing a design
  value.
* **Light-mode `ring` takes the violet**, not `brand-focus`. `#a78bfa` is specified for a
  near-black ground, where it is 7.27:1; on the ivory canvas it falls to **2.57:1** and fails the
  3:1 minimum for a non-text indicator. The violet is 5.38:1 there.

### §204.5 · Light mode is where I declined to invent

The contract requires `light`. The authorities ship **no light palette** — the Dart builds
`HelixThemeBuilder.dark` only, and `admin.tokens.css` is a dark token set. So light keeps its
existing warm-ivory neutrals and its AA-darkened status colours exactly: none were lime-derived,
and replacing them would have meant issuing a light palette the design system has not. Only the
lime values moved, plus `textOnAccent` — `#0A0C0F` on violet is **3.70:1** and had to go.

A prior commit, `ac75b42`, had raised `textMuted` for WCAG AA, so I checked the authoritative
values against that commitment **before** writing rather than after: `#8B8595` is 5.55:1 on canvas
and 5.24:1 on elevated. The authority and the accessibility commitment did not conflict. Had they,
that would have been an owner boundary, not something to resolve quietly.

### §204.6 · The check, and the three controls that prove it is not vacuous

`scripts/check-12circle-theme.ts` — **67 assertions, 67 passing**. Deliberately **not** a
snapshot: a snapshot would have frozen lime just as happily. It asserts the theme against the
transcribed authority table; **re-derives all 33 base declarations and both dark blocks from the
theme object through `CSS_VAR`**, so the *mapping* is proven rather than the emitter's agreement
with itself; runs real WCAG math on eight contrast pairs; and sha256-pins the other three themes
to the pre-change build.

This run has twice produced detectors that passed for the wrong reason — SEC-G9's case-sensitive
`can\w*`, and the reporter-dependent `Failing tests:` block of §202. So the check was made to
fail on purpose, three ways:

| control | result |
|---|---|
| reintroduce the lime accent | **FAIL 57/67** — named accent, both rings, and 1.41:1 contrast |
| restore spring easing + pill button | **FAIL 64/67** — named radius and the `1.56` overshoot |
| perturb an unrelated theme | **FAIL 66/67** — `tierstrum.css` sha256 moved |

All three exit 1. The restored tree returns to 67/67.

### §204.7 · `Q5` reassessed — the blocker is cleared, and the question was two questions

The owner gated this: *"Reassess Q5 (Phosphor) only after violet theme alignment is verified."*
It is verified, so the reassessment is due.

The consolidated pack withheld a recommendation on `Q5` for a **stated** reason: *"It also
interacts with `Q16` — if the canonical Helix artefact is settled first, the icon question may be
answered there rather than here."* **That condition has now been met.** §11547 records the handoff
declaring ***one*** shared identity — *"violet `#7C3AED`, Schibsted, **Phosphor**, 4.5:1, 44px"* —
and three of that bundle's five elements are now implemented and asserted in the registered theme.
Phosphor is the one remaining **asset** element of an identity that is no longer in question.

What the reassessment adds is that `Q5` is **two dependency decisions, not one**, and the pack put
them under a single heading:

* **Helix (TS/React).** There is **no icon dimension in Helix at all** — `src/components` is
  `Button`, `Card`, `MetricReadout`, and the string `icon` occurs **once** in `src/`, in a doc
  comment about `textOnAccent`. Adopting Phosphor here means **adding a dimension to the core**,
  and by §11547 it *"binds whatever consumes Helix next"*. This is the design-system decision the
  pack correctly refused to take in passing — and `Q16` did **not** resolve it. Resolving the
  canonical *brand* did not authorize a *dependency*.
* **12 Circle mobile (Flutter).** `pubspec.yaml` carries **only** `cupertino_icons: ^1.0.8`.
  The inventory at `931218b` names **Phosphor v2.1.1, 107 icons**, `regular` default / `fill` for
  selected — led by `ph-caret-down` (154 uses) and `ph-arrow-right` (42). Today **one** icon is
  substituted, and the substitution is recorded.

**Status: `Q5` is unblocked but still the owner's.** Its options are unchanged — `1` adopt and
match the specification · `2` keep substitutions and record each deviation · `3` vendor only the
icons used. It blocks nothing; it is visual fidelity with every deviation recorded. What has
changed is that a recommendation would no longer be agent inference about *which identity governs*
— only about scope. The pack's three *"remains on hold behind `Q16`"* lines are now stale and are
corrected there, for the same reason §196 corrected METRIC-17: a stale line in a decision document
misleads exactly the reader it is written for.

## §205 · Q2 built — and the suite that proved it reported `PASS 0/0`

### §205.1 · The last authorized-but-unbuilt decision

Reassessing the frontier after Q16, the open item was not a new question: the consolidated pack
carried `Q2` as ***"NOT YET — authorized, not built"***, deferred only because the turn that
recorded it was instructed not to modify implementation. The ruling itself has stood since
2026-10-08:

> *"the active-user population is ALL users, with the role split PUBLISHED beside the total. Not
> clients-only and not an unexplained aggregate: the split is to be shown, so a reader can apply
> either definition."*

Built as **migration 181** on `admin_activity_overview`, closing the last of the three
sub-questions the data contract (:98) put to the owner.

### §205.2 · The obvious shape would have invented a metric

The natural columns are `active_clients` / `active_coaches` / `active_partners`. Every one of
those is a definition nobody issued. The schema's vocabulary (142) is **client · coach · vendor ·
admin · content_manager · trust_operator · erasure_executor**, and `NULL` is permitted. Deciding
that `vendor` is what the contract calls a *"partner"*, or that four staff roles collapse into
one bucket, would be exactly the agent inference the standing constraints forbid — and it would
**foreclose the choice the ruling exists to preserve**, since a reader handed pre-collapsed
buckets can no longer apply the other definition.

So the split is published as a **role → count map**. It invents no grouping, it survives a role
being added to 142's CHECK without a migration here, and the Dart label table falls through to
the raw key rather than dropping an unknown role — because a dropped bucket would make a total
stop matching its own breakdown.

Two non-roles are kept apart rather than merged into one `unknown`: **`no_profile`** (no
`user_profiles` row at all — legitimate for the sign-in basis, since 142:113-115 says the ledger
*"must accept actors that were never users"*) and **`unrecorded`** (a row exists and `role` is
NULL — reachable, because 115 added the CHECK but no NOT NULL). A missing profile and an unset
column are different findings.

### §205.3 · §19.3 was checked, not assumed

The sign-in basis joins `audit_events.actor_id` to `user_profiles`, and §19.3 forbids any standing
resolver of pseudonyms. The join is nonetheless clean, and the reason is a column boundary that is
easy to misread: **142:113 states the actor identifiers *"are therefore stored raw"***, and the
pseudonym is the **next** column, `subject_pseudonym`. §19.3's prohibition — which 142:313-317
applies to the active-coach arm — concerns resolving *that*, and it is not read here. Only counts
leave the view. Had `actor_id` been the pseudonym, this basis could not have been split at all,
and the honest outcome would have been a boundary rather than a workaround.

### §205.4 · The equality is the whole point

A split that merely sits beside a total is the *"unexplained aggregate"* the ruling forbids — two
numbers that look related and are not. So the load-bearing assertion is

```
sum(the map's values) === the total column
```

for all three windows on both bases. Each map carries the **same** `admin_can` gate as the total
it splits, so a `Users`-only role sees the Session split and **NULL — not `{}`** — for the
sign-in split: an empty map is a measured emptiness, and a card that rendered the first as the
second would tell a reader *"nobody signed in"* when the truth is that they may not know.

D22 asserts it, and then **moves the population** so the equality cannot pass on two zeroes
agreeing with each other: a real session takes `session_users_today` 0 → 1 while the `client`
bucket goes 0 → 1, the sum still matches, and the asserted teardown returns both to baseline.
**25/25.**

### §205.5 · And the suite's first full-run result was `PASS 0/0`

Standalone, D22 was 25/25. Inside `run.mjs` it printed:

```
  PASS  D22   activity role split Q2 (181)     0/0
```

It ended with a bare `run();` where every other suite ends `export default await run();`. The
runner does `(await import(path)).default ?? 0`, so **two independent silences agreed on a
green**: the missing default export scored `failures = 0`, and `results.length` was read before
the un-awaited async body had registered anything. The run total stayed at its previous value and
nothing anywhere said a suite had contributed nothing.

This is the §203 lesson in a new place — *"green and meaningless"* — and the same family as
SEC-G9's vacuous `can\w*` and §202's reporter-dependent control. Three times now the defect has
been a check that could not fail, so the runner was changed as well as the suite: a suite that
registers **zero** assertions is now named **`EMPTY`**, reported on its own line with the exact
cause, and **fails the run**.

### §205.6 · The first version of that fix was itself cosmetic

Marking the suite `EMPTY` in the **printing** loop changed the word on the screen and left
`process.exit(totalFailures ? 1 : 0)` reading a total that had already been summed. The control
caught it:

```
  EMPTY D22   activity role split Q2 (181)     0 assertions — REGISTERED NOTHING
  EXIT CODE = 0
```

**A guard that reports without failing is not a guard** — and it would have gone to CI looking
fixed. The flag is now set in the collection loop before any total is computed; `EMPTY` is
subtracted from the assertion arithmetic like `ABORT` at §28.9, because neither is an assertion
failure and both are incomplete runs. Re-controlled: **exit code 1**.

### §205.7 · Results, and one count that moved on its own

| | |
|---|---|
| Live suite | **1114/1114 across 22 suites** (D22 **25/25**), Node 20, one runner at a time |
| Flutter | **1982 passed / 5 skipped** — the previous 1972 plus D22's ten Dart assertions |
| `dart analyze` | **0 errors, 0 warnings** (296 pre-existing `info`) |
| QA frontier | **181** |

`D-02` moved **39 → 40 → 39** across runs, and it is not drift: `d02:137` skips its public-signup
assertion when Supabase returns **429** on the project email rate limit. On the run that was not
limited, *"public signup cannot mint an admin"* **ran and passed** — one extra real security
assertion, not one fewer. Chasing it was still right; an unexplained count change is how §203
started.

A note on the method, recorded because it cost real time: the Flutter suite would not have run at
all. The volume was at **99% with 347 MiB free**, which on this machine makes `flutter test` hang
with no output rather than fail. Reclaiming this project's own `build` and `flutter_build` caches
bought 839 MiB and the suite ran. The 10 GB in other applications' caches was **left alone** — a
determination already recorded in memory: deleting another application's cache is the owner's
call, not an autonomous one.

**Production was not contacted.** The only database written was QA, confirmed by matching the
linked project ref against `QA_URL` before pushing the migration.

### §205.8 · And CI caught the half of the migration I had not declared

`ca2bbb6` went red on **Static guards**, and the finding was mine:

```
[rule 7] [qa] authored migration 181 is above the frontier 180 and is declared
nowhere — declare it pending (with a reason and a gate) or move the frontier
```

`supabase/expected_applied.json` still read `applied_through: "180"`. I had applied 181 to QA,
re-run the whole live suite against it and asserted it 25 ways — and left the **declaration**
behind. ENV-3's own rule is *"the frontier can only move when reality and intent move together"*,
and I had moved only reality.

The guard is a two-way comparison, so this is the direction that fails **loudly**: a version
applied without being declared. The quiet direction — declared without being applied — is the
one that would have passed CI while describing a database that does not exist. Both are the same
defect, and it is worth naming which side I landed on, because only one of them tells you.

Fixed by moving the frontier to **181**, which is the truthful declaration: it is applied, and
D22 proves it is applied. The guard's instruction — *"never delete the declaration to make this
green"* — was not needed, but it is the reason the manifest is a manifest and not a log.

**The sequence is now four steps, not three.** §188.6 recorded *"apply a migration and commit its
test together"*. That is still incomplete:

> apply → **declare the frontier** → re-run the whole live suite → commit all of it together.

The downstream jobs — Live QA among them — were **skipped**, not passed, so the earlier
green from `8f2c0c0` said nothing about this commit. All thirteen static guards were run locally
before the fix was pushed.

## §206 · Q5 adopted, Helix got CI it cannot run, and a closure that had no guard

### §206.1 · The version in the specification belonged to a different package

`Q5` closed as **Option 1 — adopt Phosphor to match the approved specification**, subject to
compatibility, licensing, package-impact and architecture checks. The handoff names *"Phosphor
Icons **v2.1.1**"*, so the first pin was `@phosphor-icons/react@2.1.1` — and **106 of the 107**
approved icons resolved.

The missing one was **`ph-calendar-dots`**, used **7** times. It is not a react-vs-web gap:
`@phosphor-icons/web@2.1.1` **has** it. The two packages version **independently**, and
`react@2.1.1` ships **1260** glyphs against the icon set's full complement. ***"v2.1.1" names the
icon set, not the React package.*** Pinned **2.1.10** (3045 glyphs): **107/107**.

**Matching the specified GLYPHS is what matching the specification means.** A spec-literal pin of
a version string belonging to a different package would have satisfied the sentence and lost an
icon — and lost it *silently*, because 106/107 looks like success. The guard now asserts
`CalendarDots` **by name**, so a future bump cannot reintroduce the gap quietly.

### §206.2 · The other three checks, and the one that nearly got papered over

| check | finding |
|---|---|
| **Licensing** | MIT, both distributions. No conflict. |
| **Compatibility** | `ERESOLVE` on first install: Phosphor peers **`react-dom`**, which Helix did not have, so npm resolved `react-dom@19` against the existing `react@18.3.1`. |
| **Maintenance** | actively published (2.1.10, 2025-05-22). |
| **Bundle impact** | measured, not asserted: **1 icon + `<Icon>` = 2,621 B raw / 1,124 B gzip**; all **102** unique approved glyphs = **320,776 B / 72,856 B gzip**. The 57 MB on disk never reaches a consumer's bundle. |

The compatibility failure handed me two buttons marked `--force` and `--legacy-peer-deps`, and
npm's own error says they *"accept an incorrect (and potentially broken) dependency resolution"*.
The real finding was a **missing peer**: Helix declared `react` and not `react-dom`. Declaring it
(dev `^18.3.1`, peer `>=18`) fixes the cause. Overriding peer resolution would have hidden it and
left every consumer to rediscover it.

### §206.3 · The boundary question the owner asked me to verify

`@phosphor-icons/react`, not `@phosphor-icons/web` — **against** the surface evidence, which
points the other way: the inventory writes **web class names** (`ph ph-arrow-right`) and `2.1.1`
matches the web package exactly. The glyphs are identical in either distribution, so the
specification is satisfied by both, and the decision turns on which boundary this package can
actually hold. Helix ships React components against a React peer, so the icon belongs in the
component tier — and the React package buys three things a webfont cannot: **per-icon
tree-shaking** instead of all-or-nothing (the 72 KB above is the whole approved set), a
**compile-time error** on a wrong glyph instead of a silently-misspelled class string, and an
**accessibility contract enforceable in code** rather than requested in a document.

Phosphor was **not** added to Flutter. The owner scoped that separately and it stays separate.

### §206.4 · The core stayed neutral, and that is asserted rather than claimed

`SemanticIconSizeTokens` is **optional**, so the three other themes received no icon tier and
their generated CSS is **byte-identical** — which the existing sha256 pins proved on the first
run, before I wrote an assertion for it. `<Icon>` knows the icon *set* and no product's icon
*choices*: the caller passes the glyph, the size comes from whichever theme is on the DOM.

12 Circle's **15 / 17 / 18px** are transcribed from the published tokens and are deliberately
**not** the 44px control size. A glyph box and a touch target are different specs — `[A]` declares
both — and conflating them is how an icon button fails a target-size audit while looking correct.
The guard asserts none of the three equals `44px`.

Checks **67 → 88**, negative-controlled three ways: the glyph box set to 44px, the pin loosened to
a range, and the icon tier handed to `tierstrum`. Each fails by name with exit 1, and the last
trips the **neutrality assertion and the sha256 pin independently** — two unrelated detections of
one violation.

One self-inflicted defect, recorded because it is the third of its kind: the *"hard-codes no
product glyph"* assertion first failed by matching **its own JSDoc example**. SEC-G9 flagged its
own documentation; §203's sweep fired on the sentence explaining an absence; this did both. It now
strips comments first **and asserts that the strip worked**.

### §206.5 · Helix now has CI, and it cannot run

A workflow was added: `npm ci` → `typecheck` → `build` → `check:12circle`, Node 20, no secrets, no
matrix, no publish. It also runs `scripts/selftest-12circle-guard.sh`, which reinstates the lime
accent **in the workspace copy only**, asserts the check rejects it, restores, and re-asserts
green. Nothing broken is committed.

The self-test asserts **why** the check failed, not merely that it did, and a meta-control proved
that distinction earns its keep: with the guard deliberately **blinded** to lime and to its accent
table, the check **still exited non-zero** for incidental reasons — the contrast assertions. *A
self-test reading only the exit code would have passed a guard that had stopped guarding.*

**The workflow cannot execute.** Both runs failed before any step, and the annotation is an
account matter, not a defect:

> *"The job was not started because recent account payments have failed or your spending limit
> needs to be increased."*

`akutonsol/12circlefitness` is **public** — free Actions minutes, which is why its CI runs.
`helix-design-system` is **private**, and consumes paid minutes. Substituted evidence, per the
owner's `LOCALLY_VERIFIED` instruction: a **fresh clone of `e1c0891`** on **Node 20**, running the
workflow's exact step sequence. All steps pass, **88/88**, zero lime in the generated CSS. Marked
**`LOCALLY_VERIFIED`**, not green. Resolving the billing block, or changing the repository's
visibility, is the owner's.

### §206.6 · A `VERIFIED_CLOSED` P1 with no standing guard

Reassessing the frontier turned up a line in `MASTER_PRODUCT_DECISIONS.md` row `PD-A05`: ***"Not
yet implemented: applied migration 125 implements option (b)."*** It reads like unbuilt authorized
work. **It is stale.** 125 implemented option (b); migration **128** superseded it with the ruled
option (a), and `F-J-12` is `VERIFIED_CLOSED` with all four SECURITY/AUTHORIZATION states present.
**Nothing needed building, and the investigation is what established that** — acting on the line
would have meant re-implementing a closed finding.

That register is under a standing do-not-modify constraint, so the stale line is **reported, not
corrected**. It needs the owner.

The same row carries a **retained limitation** that is *not* stale:

> *"RLS policies are outside the I-MIG-03 durability guard, which tracks function properties
> only — this closure has **no standing guard** against silent replacement."*

Migration 128 says it of itself, naming the mechanism: *"the exact mechanism that produced
F-J-01."* `SEC-G1` already pins the `F-21` policy family, so a test-level policy guard is
established practice — and 128 and registry §7.11 both record whether **Gate 0.14** should cover
policies as an open **governance** question, so the gate was left alone. Pinning a shape the owner
already ruled does not decide it.

**`SEC-G11`** (`decision_trace_read_scope_guard_test.dart`, 14 assertions) pins option (a) arm by
arm: the four authorized arms present, `is_active_coach_of(subject_id)` **scoped to the subject**,
the admin arm on the pinned `public.is_admin()` rather than 125's inline `EXISTS`,
`content_manager` not granted, no bare role-class arm, `TO authenticated`, **no write policy on
`decision_traces` in any migration in the tree**, and no table-level `GRANT` to a role class. It
also carries the **D-3 definer ratchet**: the set of migrations defining these policies is
recorded, and a new one fails the guard until its shape is reviewed.

### §206.7 · The guard caught two of my own errors before I committed it

**The definer list was wrong.** I derived `[089, 128]` from a shell `grep`; the Dart detector found
**`[089, 125, 128]`**. 125 defines the policy too, and my grep's pattern missed it. The weaker tool
produced the input and the stronger one rejected it.

**And the `content_manager` assertion was the digit-sweep trap again.** It failed on stripped SQL —
because the word survives in `COMMENT ON POLICY … IS '…content_manager is deliberately NOT
granted…'`, which is a **string literal, not a comment**. The fix was *not* to strip literals:
`role IN ('coach')` is a literal that matters, and removing literals would have blinded the arm
that detects F-J-12 itself. The grant assertions are scoped to the `CREATE POLICY` statement, and
the meta-test now states the real property — stripping removes the header occurrences, exactly one
survives in the COMMENT, and the **grant** mentions it nowhere.

Negative-controlled by adding a **throwaway later migration** that widens the policy — never by
editing an applied one, which §8 forbids. **10 of 14 assertions fail**, exit 1, naming
`content_manager`, the unscoped coach arm, the inline `EXISTS`, the bare role class, the write
policy and the ratchet. The file was deleted and the frontier confirmed back at 181.

### §206.8 · Where the frontier actually stands

`DESIGN-01` and `DESIGN-02` are **`STATUS — DESIGN AUTHORITY REQUIRED`** in their own governing
document: the missing artifacts are *state frames* and *per-component specification sheets*, and
the alternative on offer is a **ruling** that the six screens suffice. Both are design-authority
decisions. Adding the `Icon` component moved Helix from 3 of ≈30 components to 4 — but
`DESIGN-02`'s gap is the **specification**, not the implementation, and counting a component I
derived without a spec as progress against it would be the inference the constraints forbid.

Every `METRIC-*` decision is now resolved **and** built; `Q2` at §205 was the last. The sweep for
*"authorized but not built"* returns nothing, which is why this section's executable work came
from a **retained limitation** rather than from the decision queue.

Three stale status lines were corrected in the decision pack — `Q7`/`D-1` still read *"NOT YET —
authorized, not built"*, `EC-01 Q5` still read *"awaiting Approve / Deny"*, and the Q16 boundary
paragraph still read *"implementation-pending"*. All three describe work that is done. Same reason
as §196 and §204.7: a stale line in a decision document misleads exactly the reader it is for.

**Production was not contacted.**

### §206.9 · The four assertions that did NOT fire, and what two of them revealed

The control fired 10 of SEC-G11's 14 assertions. Asking which four stayed silent — rather than
being satisfied with "it failed" — found two real weaknesses. The per-test verdicts came from
`--reporter json`, so each is named rather than inferred from a count.

| assertion | why it passed | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| the migration corpus is found and non-trivial | the tree was readable, which is the point | **expected negative** |
| comment stripping removes the prose but not the policy COMMENT | pins **128's own text**, which the probe never touched | **expected negative** |
| no migration `GRANT`s `decision_traces` to a role class | the probe used a **POLICY**; a `GRANT` is a different vector | **gap — untested** |
| "declares exactly one policy" | read `definers.last`, which under a widening **is the widening migration** — and it declared one policy of its own | **gap — weak** |

The first two must pass. The corpus check is the vacuity guard: if it ever fails alongside the
others, the ten failures mean *"the tree could not be read"*, not *"a widening was detected"* —
so the control asserts it **passed**, which is the difference between evidence and noise.

The other two were defects.

**The `GRANT` arm had never been seen to fail.** By this programme's own standard that made it
decoration. A second probe — `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE public.decision_traces TO content_manager` —
fires it, and fires **exactly one** assertion, which is the result worth having: a table-level
grant does not change the policy's shape, so anything else failing would have been a false
positive. The control now asserts that narrowness, so it tests both the detection and the
absence of over-detection.

**And "exactly one policy" was asserting about the wrong file.** Written against
`definers.last`, it followed the frontier — so under attack it inspected the attacker's own
migration and passed. The ratchet still caught the widening, so nothing was unguarded; but the
assertion was not asserting what it claimed. It now pins migration **128 by number**. An
assertion about 128 should name 128.

Both probes are throwaway **later** migrations, never edits to an applied one, and both are
removed with the frontier re-confirmed at 181.

### §206.10 · The full Flutter suite did not run here — and why that is recorded, not waived

The local full-suite run **hung for 2 h 43 m and was killed**. It was not a test failure: free
space had fallen to **127 MiB**, which on this machine makes `flutter test` stop producing output
and never return — the behaviour already recorded in memory, now observed a second time at a
larger scale because clearing `.dart_tool/flutter_build` forced a cold recompile.

What the volume actually holds was measured rather than assumed: `/private/var/folders` carries
**2.5 GB**, of which **1.4 GB is Chrome's `code_sign_clone`** and **475 MB is Docker Desktop's
update payload** — other applications' data, and not an autonomous deletion. `~/.dartServer`
(439 MB) and the node/tsx caches were toolchain caches and were reclaimed; the Flutter SDK's own
3.3 GB cache was left alone because deleting it breaks `flutter` until a full re-download.

So the honest split:

* **VERIFIED locally** — SEC-G11 **14/14**, the Q2 model group **30/30** (44 tests in the two
  touched files), the two-vector negative control **exit 0**, `dart analyze lib test` **0 errors**.
* **NOT RUN locally** — the remaining ~1950 tests of the full suite. **`LOCALLY_VERIFIED`, not
  green**, and not claimed otherwise.

The full suite is not skipped: CI's `flutter` job runs it on a clean runner with no disk
constraint, and `12circlefitness` is public so its Actions minutes are free. That is the
authoritative full-suite result, and it is reported against the actual commit rather than
inferred from a previous one.

### §206.11 · The other retained limitation, and a blocker that had already lifted

`F-J-12` carried **two** retained limitations. §206.6 took (i). This is (ii):

> *"J-04A's `created_by=neq` filter is NULL-rejecting, so a readable `created_by IS NULL` trace
> would be invisible to that negative control (none is readable under option (a) today)."*

**The filter did not mean what its name said.** J-04A asserts that an unrelated coach cannot read
traces they did not create, and the `neq` narrowing was deliberate and correct in intent — `d05`
§9 probe D creates one trace per run that this coach *did* create, so the unfiltered form had
stopped testing its own proposition. But `neq` is NULL-rejecting in PostgREST, and **a trace with
no creator is also one the coach did not create.** The filter is now
`or=(created_by.is.null,created_by.neq.<coach>)`.

This is a reachable shape, not a hypothetical: 089 declares `created_by uuid references
user_profiles(id)` with **no NOT NULL**, and no later migration alters it. **Adding NOT NULL would
be a data-contract decision and was not taken.**

**And the parenthetical is now an assertion.** *"(none is readable under option (a) today)"* was a
measurement nobody re-ran. It runs every time now, and through the **authorized** read path rather
than a service key: `admin` holds the admin arm, so a NULL-creator trace readable at all would be
visible to it. Both query shapes were validated against QA by read-only request before commit —
the `or=` form returns 200 with rows, `created_by=is.null` returns `[]` — so the widened filter
changes no result today and the new assertion holds. Verification is CI's, whose Live QA job runs
`npm run test:ai`; running it locally would have contended for the same QA project.

### §206.12 · `FG-3` looked executable, and checking why it was not found three stale records

The retained-limitation sweep turned up a fourth candidate on the `SEC-R1` row:

> *"the row's Live QA field also names the positive legs (owning coach → 200, `service_role` →
> 200); **no suite asserts them, so an over-refusing wrapper would look identical to a correct
> one**."*

That is a serious gap — **with only the negative legs asserted, a wrapper that refused everyone
would pass** — and it is registered as `FG-3`. It is also **not mine to take**: the table it sits
in is headed *"recorded, NOT implemented (owner assignment required, no silent scope expansion)"*,
and implementing it anyway is the expansion that sentence forbids. So it is requested, not built.

**Reading that header is what found the real finding.** It governs `FG-1` and `FG-2` too — and
both have been implemented for some time. The blocker all three were waiting on, a QA **database**

| marker, CI run `38194730786` step *Live SQL evidence* (**`success`**) | |
|---|---|
| `QA_DB_URL: ***` in the job env | the credential is provisioned |
| `FG-1 · function search_path posture (SEC-09 live half)` | `FG-1` ran |
| `FG-2a · Phase 2 workout contract` · `FG-2b · generated plan day titles` | `FG-2` ran |
| `ENV-3 · declared vs observed vs authored` | `ENV-3`'s live half ran |

**A `success` conclusion alone would not have proved this**, and that is the methodological point:

`::notice title=Live SQL evidence skipped::…`. The distinction is that the notice is **absent** and

Three records still described the blocker as live. One of them —
