## §207 · Three decisions made answerable — and `FG-3` is under-specified in four ways

No implementation this section. The frontier was already at the owner boundary, so the work was to
make each remaining decision answerable without the owner re-deriving the evidence.

### §207.1 · `FG-3` cannot be implemented as written, and the reasons are not pedantic

`FG-3` asks for *"the owning coach → 200 and `service_role` → 200 for each of the five
wrappers"*. Four things stop that being a build instruction:

**Two of the five wrappers have no owning coach.** The class splits by predicate, which `FG-3`'s
wording does not capture: `evaluate_week`, `regenerate_program` and `materialize_program_week`
guard on `can_act_on_program(p_program_id)`; **`predict_client` and `assemble_weekly_review` guard
on `can_act_for(p_subject)`** — no program, no coach_id, nothing to own. The authorized positive
caller for that pair is a different question with a different answer.

**A naive positive probe would pass without testing anything.** Both predicates admit a NULL
scope, and say so in their own comments — `program IS NULL`, and `subject IS NULL -- unscoped call,
subject defaulted`. These are documented design, not defects; they keep optional-parameter call
sites working and let the internal engine call through. But a probe that passes NULL **takes its
200 from the NULL arm**. The existing negative probe depends on the mirror-image property, passing
a non-program uuid so the predicate is false. So the positive contract has to require a *real*
owned program, and that has to be stated rather than assumed.

**`service_role → 200` is not authorization evidence.** It passes via the
`(SELECT auth.uid()) IS NULL` arm — the internal-engine arm. It would pass identically if every
relationship arm were deleted. It proves the engine path is reachable, which is liveness.

**And "→ 200" is not sufficient by this repository's own rule** that an HTTP status alone never
proves a write. Each wrapper delegates to an engine that writes to `decision_traces`,
`communications`, `predictions` or `program_versions`. A no-op engine returns 200 too.

### §207.2 · The part only the owner can resolve: the closure standard disagrees with itself here

`QA_CLOSURE_STANDARD.md` §2.1 defines **VERIFIED LIVE** as a real request that reproduces the
correct behaviour *"**and the same probe demonstrably failed before the fix**"*.

**A positive leg cannot satisfy that.** Before the fix the wrapper had **no guard** — so the owning
coach got **200 then as well**. The pre-fix state was *more* permissive, not less. There is no
pre-fix failure to show, and manufacturing one would mean reverting an applied migration, which §8
forbids.

The definition is written for **denial** evidence. A positive leg is the opposite shape, and
`FG-3` is a positive leg. That is a governance question, not an engineering one, and it is the
reason `FG-3`'s registry row insists on owner assignment rather than listing a task.

What *was* established, so the assignment is cheap: `KNOWN_OPEN` is now **`[]`** — migration 124
restored the last stripped guard, so no member is exempt from probing any more — and a coach-owned
`workout_programs` fixture is already established practice in `d05` and `d17`. The fixture
mechanism is not the blocker. **The side effects are**: a positive probe executes the engine and
writes to tables other suites measure, `decision_traces` among them at 979 rows. `d04` §8 already
declined to run such a probe once, on exactly that reasoning.

Written up as `V5_FG3_DECISION_REQUEST.md`. **`FG-3` is not closed and nothing was implemented.**

### §207.3 · `DESIGN-02` was one question that cannot be answered once

The ruling on offer — *"the six screens are sufficient specification"* — silently decides two
different things, and one of them it cannot decide at all. Split into:

* **`D2-1`** · are the screens authoritative for the **24** components they depict? That ratifies
  `COMPONENT-SPECS.md`'s derivation, or replaces it with a designed sheet. Its real consequence is
  whether a later visual correction is a **change** or a **bug**.
* **`D2-2`** · what governs the **nine** they do not depict? Measured across the six
  non-superseded `screens/*.dc.html` at `931218b`, all nine return **zero** occurrences — `toast`,
  `skeleton`, `type="radio"`, `date`, `timeline`, `read-only`, `permission`, `audit row`,
  `before/after`/`diff`. **A component absent from the screens cannot be derived from them**, so
  "the screens suffice" leaves these nine with *no* authority rather than derived authority.

`D2-2` carries an option worth naming because it costs nothing: three of the nine are `A11` state
surfaces — `skeleton`, `permission-denied panel`, `read-only banner` — which
`SCREEN-INVENTORY.md` already designs as **patterns** while `COMPONENTS.md` also lists them as
**components**. Ruling that the pattern *is* the specification for those three closes the overlap
without inventing anything and narrows the open set from nine to six.

### §207.4 · Helix: the minimum action is a billing fix, and `main` turns out to be unprotected

The hosted-CI blocker is an account matter — *"recent account payments have failed or your
spending limit needs to be increased"* — and the asymmetry is explained: `12circlefitness` is
**public** (free minutes), `helix-design-system` is **private** (paid). The minimum owner action
is resolving Actions billing. **Making the repository public would also work and is NOT the
minimum**: it is a disclosure decision, it needs explicit authorization, and it is not offered as
a default.

Two things worth recording for whoever reads the PRs next.

**The failure is indistinguishable from a real one in the UI**, and distinguishable in exactly one
place: a genuine failure has step conclusions, this has `steps: []`. `gh run view --log` returns
*"log not found"*. The annotation is only reachable through
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/check-runs/<job_id>/annotations`.

**And `main` carries no branch protection** — `404 Branch not protected`, so no required status
checks. The failing check is therefore **advisory**: both PRs report `MERGEABLE` /
`UNSTABLE`, where the single `FAILURE` is the job that never started. **That makes merging
possible, not advisable**, and not mine to do — it would land changes whose only hosted evidence is
a job that never ran. Neither PR was merged.

Q16 and Q5 were re-verified in place rather than assumed from the checkpoint: build exit 0,
**88/88**, generated CSS carrying the violet and **zero** lime, the four-theme registry intact with
`12circle` distinct from `12circle-communities`, Phosphor pinned exactly at `2.1.10` with
`CalendarDots` and all eight `fill`-weight glyphs resolving.

**Production was not contacted.** No probe was run against QA for any of this beyond read-only
inspection of committed source.

## §208 · `ec03`'s control had §202's defect too, and CI is where it was silent

### §208.1 · Found by sweeping, not by accident

§202 fixed `secw1`'s reporter dependence: it keyed a verdict off Flutter's `Failing tests:` block,
which the **GitHub reporter CI attaches does not print**, so two assertions would have passed
**vacuously** in CI. That was fixed and the lesson recorded — but the lesson was never applied to
the other controls.

Sweeping all fourteen negative-control scripts for the same shape found exactly one more:
**`ec03_negative_control.sh`**, wired into CI at `ci.yml:422`.

```bash
FAILING="$(printf '%s\n' "$OUTPUT" | sed -n '/^Failing tests:/,$p')"
if printf '%s\n' "$FAILING" | grep -Fq "$ARM_FAILED_SAVE"; then
  die "the mutation also broke the failed-save arm …"
fi
echo "only the session-lost arm failed, exactly as declared"
```

Under the GitHub reporter there is no such section, so `FAILING` is **empty**, the `grep` matches
nothing, the `if` is false, and the script prints *"only the session-lost arm failed, exactly as
declared"* **having checked nothing at all.** The one direction that could not work is the one that
matters: the proof that the mutation did not reach further than declared.

**The positive direction was weak too**, and that was not previously noticed:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "$OUTPUT" | grep -Fq "$ARM_SESSION" || die "expected EC-03 failure not observed"
```

Grepping the output for an arm's **name** matches when the test merely **runs** — every reporter
prints the name on pass and on fail alike. So the "expected failure observed" assertion was
satisfied by the test existing.

### §208.2 · Both directions now read per-test results

Converted to `--reporter json`, the same instrument `secw1` and `SEC-G11` use, and the verdicts are
per-test `result` values rather than summary prose. It is strictly stronger than the original
intent in two ways: the failed-save arm must be **present and `success`**, not merely absent from a
block; and an arm that did not run at all is a **failure** — *absence is not evidence, because a
renamed or deleted test would otherwise read as success.*

### §208.3 · Verified by fixture, because the machine could not run it — and CI is the right place anyway

The volume fell to **133 MiB** during the baseline leg and the run stalled in the §205.10 hang
mode; it was killed. `intake_flow_screen.dart` was confirmed **clean** — the kill landed before the
mutation leg, and the script's `EXIT` trap held.

So the verdict logic was tested directly, by driving the extracted analyzer with synthetic
reporter output:

| fixture | required | observed |
|---|---|---|
| session arm failed · failed-save passed | accept | **exit 0** |
| **both** arms failed | reject — reached further | **exit 1** |
| session arm **passed** | reject — under-reached | **exit 1** |
| the arm **never ran** | reject — absence is not evidence | **exit 1** |
| **empty** reporter output | reject | **exit 1** |

The last row is the whole point: **an empty parse was the old CI condition**, and it used to print
a pass. It is now a hard failure.

End-to-end verification belongs to CI regardless of the disk, because **CI is the environment the
defect lived in** — the old code worked locally and was silent there. Local evidence is
`bash -n` clean plus the fixture table above; `ci.yml:422` exercises the whole harness.

**Production was not contacted.**

## §209 · The `ec03` fix left the tree mutated on every failure path

### §209.1 · I replaced the restore trap and did not notice

§208's conversion of `ec03_negative_control.sh` to the json reporter added this, at line 127:

```bash
JSON="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$JSON"' EXIT
```

**Bash keeps exactly one `EXIT` trap.** A second one *replaces* the first — so that line silently
removed the `trap cleanup EXIT` installed at line 48, the handler whose entire job is restoring
`intake_flow_screen.dart`.

The window is the worst possible one. The mutation is applied **before** line 127 and the explicit
restore is at line 187, so for sixty lines the tree was modified with **no restoring trap**. And
those sixty lines are where the analyzer lives, which can `die` five different ways. Any of them —
the session arm passing, the failed-save arm failing, an arm not running, an unparseable report,
an ambiguous name — would have exited with `intake_flow_screen.dart` **left mutated in the
working tree**.

CI never showed it, and could not: CI exercises the happy path, where line 187 restores explicitly
and the run goes green. The defect is only reachable on a failure, which is precisely when a
negative control matters.

### §209.2 · Proved by reproduction, not by reading

A nine-line pair, no Flutter, no disk:

| shape | exit | the file afterwards |
|---|---|---|
| second `trap … EXIT` after the mutation | 1 | **`MUTATED`** — left modified |
| one trap carrying both responsibilities | 1 | `original` — **restored** |

### §209.3 · Fixed, and the class swept

`cleanup()` now removes the reporter file too, and the second `trap` is gone — with a comment at
both sites saying why, because the mistake is invisible unless you know bash replaces rather than
appends.

All **fifteen** control and evidence scripts were then swept for the same shape. Thirteen carry
exactly one `EXIT` trap. One carries two — `i3a11`, at `77:trap restore EXIT` and
`112:trap - EXIT` — and it is **correct**: it calls `restore` explicitly at 111 and *then* disarms,
so the three `die` paths below it run against an already-restored tree. Disarming after an explicit
restore is the opposite of replacing a trap before one.

**So `ec03` was the only instance, and I wrote it.** That is the second defect this programme has
found inside a fix for a defect — §205.6 was the first, where the `EMPTY`-suite guard was marked in
the printing loop and left `process.exit` reading a stale total. Both share a shape: the repair was
verified against the behaviour it was built to fix, and not against the behaviour it changed.

**Production was not contacted.**

## §210 · A dead null check that silently dropped the case it was written for

### §210.1 · First, a correction to my own reporting

I have twice reported `dart analyze` as **"0 errors, 0 warnings (296 pre-existing info)"**. The
errors figure was right; **the warnings figure was wrong.** Measured properly:

| scope | error | warning | info |
|---|---|---|---|
| whole project | 0 | **19** | 296 |
| `lib/` only | 0 | **3** | 66 |

The grep I used was `^\s+(error|warning) -` and it matched nothing, which I read as "none" rather
than as "the pattern is wrong". A pattern that returns zero is indistinguishable from a clean
tree unless you check it against something it should match — the same mistake as a guard that
cannot fail, applied to my own measurement.

### §210.2 · The defect the warnings were pointing at

Two of the three `lib/` warnings sat on one line of
`active_workout_screen.dart:1364`, inside `_swapExercise`:

```dart
// The cursor pointed into the exercise that is gone. Re-point it at the
// replacement's first set so a refresh lands somewhere that exists.
if (replacement.sets.isNotEmpty &&
    (_currentSetId == null || we.setById(_currentSetId!) != null)) {
```

> *The operand can't be 'null', so the condition is always 'false'.*

And it cannot, because line **170** declares `String _currentSetId = '';` — **non-nullable, with
the empty string as its "no cursor yet" sentinel.**

So the `== null` arm was dead, and the case it was written for fell through to
`we.setById('')`, which compares `''` against every set id, matches nothing, and returns null.
**The condition was false exactly when it needed to be true.** A client who swapped an exercise
*before touching any set* kept a cursor pointing into the exercise that had just been removed —
the precise failure the comment above it says it prevents.

Not caught by tests, and the reason is worth recording: `workout_domain_contract_test.dart` has
five `replacedBy` tests, so the swap *looks* covered. They test the **model's** swap. The screen's
cursor logic had no coverage at all.

### §210.3 · Fixed as a predicate, because a condition cannot be tested

The decision is now `shouldRepointCursor(currentSetId:, replaced:, replacement:)` — three lines,
no widget, ordered so the `sets.isEmpty` arm stays first because the caller reads `sets.first`
immediately. The call site shrank to one call.

`workout_cursor_repoint_test.dart` asserts six things: no-cursor re-points (**the case that was
broken**), a cursor inside the replaced exercise re-points, a cursor elsewhere is left alone, an
empty replacement never re-points under either cursor state, and two **premise ratchets** — that
the field is still a non-nullable `String` with an empty-string sentinel, and that the call site
no longer compares the cursor to null. If someone makes the field nullable, the first test stops
testing the real path, so the ratchet fails instead.

Each negative test asserts its own premise first (`setById(elsewhere)` **is** null; the
replacement's sets **are** empty), so none of them can pass because the fixture was wrong.

The third `lib/` warning was a `duplicate_import` in `daily_checkin_screen.dart` — one line, and
`lib/` is now at **0 warnings**.

## §212 · `FG-3`'s mirror image, which needed no decision at all

### §212.1 · The five facts, re-verified in source

`V5_FG3_DECISION_REQUEST.md`'s six questions were re-checked against the tree rather than carried
forward on trust. All five supporting facts hold:

| fact | evidence |
|---|---|
| the class splits by predicate | `predict_client` · `assemble_weekly_review` → **`can_act_for(p_subject)`**; `evaluate_week` · `materialize_program_week` · `regenerate_program` → **`can_act_on_program(p_program_id)`** |
| both predicates admit a NULL scope | `program IS NULL` and `subject IS NULL -- unscoped call, subject defaulted` |
| `service_role` passes as the engine | `(SELECT auth.uid()) IS NULL -- service_role / engine`, first arm of both |
| a 200 is insufficient | each wrapper delegates to an engine writing `decision_traces` · `communications` · `predictions` · `program_versions` |
| §2.1 conflicts with a positive leg | *"…**and the same probe demonstrably failed before the fix**"* — unsatisfiable where the pre-fix wrapper had no guard |

One addition worth recording: **I-MIG-03 already tracks all five**, reporting `intact` for each
with its defining migration named (116 for four, **124** for `materialize_program_week`). So the
wrappers' *source-level* durability is guarded. What `FG-3` asks for is the *behavioural* positive
leg, and that remains owner-assigned. **No question was answered and nothing in `FG-3` was
implemented.**

### §212.2 · But the negative leg had the same defect, pointing the other way

`FG-3` says an **over-refusing** wrapper is indistinguishable from a correct one. Reading `d04`
§8's existing probe showed the mirror:

```js
check(`${fn}() refuses an unauthorized caller`, r.status >= 400, …);
```

**Any error counted as a refusal.** A malformed argument, a wrong signature, a type error or a 500
would all have read as *"the guard held"* — a **broken** wrapper indistinguishable from a
**guarding** one. That is decision-independent: the expected refusal is written in 116's own
source, `RAISE EXCEPTION … USING ERRCODE = '42501'`, and needs nobody's ruling.

Observed first, then asserted. All five return **403 · `42501`**, and the message names the
predicate that refused — *"not authorized for this **subject**"* for the `can_act_for` pair,
*"…this **program**"* for the other three.

So the probe now asserts two things per member: that the refusal is the **authorization** error
rather than merely an error, and that it came from **that member's own predicate**. The second is
the only part that can catch a wrapper which silently swapped predicates — it would still 403, and
would still be wrong, because the two guard different things.

### §212.3 · And the old assertion was vacuous in a reachable way

Two controls, both firing:

| control | result |
|---|---|
| `evaluate_week` mislabelled subject-scoped | **FAIL** — *"message=not authorized for this program (expected the subject arm)"* |
| a malformed call — one bogus argument | **FAIL** — **`404 / PGRST202` "Could not find the function"** |

The second is the point. **404 ≥ 400**, so under the previous assertion a signature that does not
exist would have passed as *"refuses an unauthorized caller"*. This was not a theoretical
weakness; it was reachable by a typo in the argument map the probe itself maintains.

`d04` **66 → 71**; live suite **1114 → 1120 across 22 suites**, the remaining +1 being `D-02`'s
documented 429 branch (40/40 on the run that was not rate-limited).

**Nothing here touches authorization semantics, and `FG-3` is no closer to closed.** It is the one
piece of `FG-3`-adjacent work that required no owner decision, and it makes the existing negative
leg mean what it already claimed.

## §213 · Helix is only billing — and a shell bug had falsified the DESIGN-02 evidence

### §213.1 · The Helix question worth answering before asking anyone to pay

Is a workflow defect hiding behind the billing refusal, so that clearing billing just reveals a
second problem? **No**, and the evidence is in what GitHub did *before* it declined:

| observation | what it rules out |
|---|---|
| a job exists, named **"Theme contract (12circle)"** — that string is the workflow's own `name:` | the YAML parsed and the job resolved |
| `steps: 0` | it never started; it did not start and fail |
| `event=pull_request` | the trigger matched |
| the only `failure` annotation is the billing message, with **no `Invalid workflow file`** | a malformed workflow emits that instead, and produces no job at all |
| every step already ran green in a clean clone on Node 20 | the step content is not the problem |

real run.

The owner action is now exact rather than generic: `akutonsol` is a **User** account
(`gh api users/akutonsol` → `"type": "User"`) owning the repository directly, so this is

### §214.2 — Workstream 5 · deferring all eight was right once and wrong seven times

The findings document deferred **all eight** `use_build_context_synchronously` sites on three
grounds: the fixes change behaviour, one is a payment flow, and `flutter test` could not run at
132 MiB. The third expired with the disk. Examining each finding **on its own terms** rather than
as a list showed the first two applied to exactly one of them.

**`coach_dashboard_screen.dart:864`** — the guard was `context.mounted` where the closure captures
the **State's** context, and for a `State` the lint wants the State's own liveness. `State.mounted`
*is* `State.context.mounted`, so the change is the idiomatic spelling, not a suppression.

**The six `Navigator.pop` sites** — the first pass worried the dialog would mount under a
different ancestor and resolve inherited widgets differently. **Reading `FoodAddedDialog.show`
settles it**: it hands the context to `showDialog` and does nothing else with it, its builder is
`(_) =>` which ignores the dialog's own context, and `FoodAddedDialog` takes plain values. **No
inherited widget is read through that context at all**, so the ancestor change cannot alter what
renders — and the hazard removed is real, because `showDialog` against a context whose route has
just been popped can raise *"Looking up a deactivated widget's ancestor"*, and only appears to
work because the lookup resolves before the pop animation finishes.

**`upgrade_screen.dart:172` stays open**, and it is the one where the code's own comment states
the consequence: *"embedded checkout navigated away"*. A guard before `launchCheckout` would
silently answer whether a client who left mid-change still gets a checkout session. That is a
billing decision, not a lint, and it is not mine.

`lib/` `use_build_context` findings **8 → 1**; `dart analyze` **0 errors · 0 warnings**; widget
suite **518**; full suite **2002 / 5 skipped**.

**Production was not contacted.**

### §214.3 · The unauthenticated leg, extended from a sample to the class

`d04` §1 probes `anon` against a **sample** of the API surface, and `predict_client` was the only
class member in it. `SEC-R1`'s *Tests* field asks for the five to be asserted *"as a class, not
individually"*, so the sample is now extended to the class — the last row of the FG-3 coverage
matrix that could be filled without an owner decision.

**And it is a different defence from the one §212 strengthened**, which is why it is worth its own
assertion rather than being folded in:

| caller | stopped by | observed |
|---|---|---|
| `anon` | the **GRANT** — the body never runs | **401** · `42501` · *"permission denied for function …"* |
| authenticated non-owner | the **PREDICATE**, inside the body | **403** · `42501` · *"not authorized for this subject/program"* |

Both carry `42501`, so a probe keyed on the code alone cannot tell them apart; it is the **status
and the message** that distinguish the layers. A test that accepted either for both would not
notice if one of the two defences disappeared.

Negative-controlled: asserting the *predicate* message for an `anon` caller fails on all five.

`d04` **71 → 76**; live suite **1124/1124 across 22 suites** (the arithmetic differs by one from
§212's figure because of `D-02`'s documented 429 branch).

## §215 · `FG-3` assigned and implemented — and a teardown that could never recover

### §215.1 · The positive legs exist now

`FG-3` was the oldest open evidence gap in the programme: five wrappers whose **denial** was
asserted and whose **admission** was not, so *"an over-refusing wrapper would look identical to a
correct one"*. The owner assigned it with six decisions, and `d23-fg3-positive-legs.mjs` now
implements them — **21/21**, live suite **1146/1146 across 23 suites**.

The design point is that a 200 proves nothing about *why*. Each leg is therefore a **pair against
the identical scope, varying only the caller**: the owning coach (or the subject) → **200**, an
unrelated authenticated user → **403 · `42501`**. Same ids, same arguments. That isolates the
relationship arm from the NULL arm, from a `service_role` bypass, from an admin shortcut, and from
a malformed signature.

`service_role` is asserted **separately and labelled in the assertion text** as liveness — it
passes through `auth.uid() IS NULL`, so it would succeed with every relationship arm deleted.

### §215.2 · Option C does not mean the same thing for all five, and I had the facts wrong

Reading the engine bodies to find out what *"the expected engine-owned row"* is produced a
correction to my own earlier claim. I had written that each wrapper *"delegates to an engine that
writes to four tables"*. **Wrong** — the four INSERTs I had seen in 116 belong to
`generate_workout`, `create_weekly_review`, `record_prediction` and `snapshot_program_version`.

What the five engines actually do: **three write nothing** (`predict_client`,
`assemble_weekly_review`, `evaluate_week` — zero mutating keywords in their bodies);
`materialize_program_week` inserts `program_workouts`; `regenerate_program` updates
`workout_programs.plan` and inserts `decision_traces`, but **only on its `applied` branch** — with
`p_approved=false` it returns `pending_approval` and writes nothing.

So for three wrappers the asserted effect is the returned payload, because a row assertion would
demand something the engine never promised. **A factual limit on option C, flagged to the owner,
not a quiet substitution.**

Two things the fixture taught, both from reading errors rather than guessing: the engine iterates
`week->'split'` and raises **22004** (*"upper bound of FOR loop cannot be null"*) on a week without
one — which is why the fixture carries a `split`; and `materialize_program_week` transitively calls
`generate_workout`, which **inserts `decision_traces`**, so teardown removes exactly the ids that
did not exist beforehand rather than issuing a blanket delete on a provenance table other suites
count.

### §215.3 · A teardown gated on the thing it was meant to clean up

A tool call was interrupted mid-run, between `D15`'s probe INSERT and its teardown. The row
survived — and `D15` then failed **on every subsequent run**, standalone and in the suite:

```
x seeded a probe integration row carrying a token — status=409
```

The cause is worse than residue. The cleanup line read:

```js
if (seededIntegration) await svc("user_integrations?provider=eq.qa-d15-probe", {method:'DELETE'});
```

`provider` is unique, so the leftover row makes the next INSERT return **409** →
`seededIntegration = false` → **the cleanup is skipped** → the row survives again. **The only code
that removes the row was gated on the thing the row prevents.** One interruption became a
permanent failure no later run could clear.

Made unconditional — deleting by `provider` is idempotent and costs nothing when there is nothing
to delete. Characterised honestly with a planted orphan:

| | |
|---|---|
| orphan present, old shape | fails **forever** |
| orphan present, new shape | **still fails that run** (342/343 — the INSERT genuinely conflicts) **but clears the row** |
| the next run | **353/353** |

The fix does not rescue the failing run. It breaks the loop. And `D15` reports **353** rather than
343 now, because a successful seed unlocks ten assertions the 409 had been skipping — so the 409
was also **suppressing coverage**, not merely failing one check.

**Production was not contacted.** The orphan row was QA probe data this session created, and it
was removed.

## §216 · The checkout lifecycle — the last analyzer finding was a real defect

### §216.1 · What the owner directed, and what the code actually did

**Owner direction, 2026-10-12:** *do not create a new checkout session after the client navigates
away from the upgrade flow* — and *do not abandon or duplicate a successfully created one.* The
two halves pull in opposite directions, which is why this needed the payment contract read rather
than a `mounted` check pasted in.

The flow in `_onCta`:

```dart
if (onMembership) {
  final result = await paymentSvc.changeMembership(p.kind!);   // ← the async gap
  if (result == 'changed') { … return; }
}
final ok = await launchCheckout(context, ref, kind: p.kind!);  // ← flagged
if (!mounted) return;
```

**What the contract says.** `changeMembership` invokes `update-subscription` and returns one of
`'changed'`, `'needs_checkout'` or `'error'`. It creates **no session** — `needsCheckout: true` is
a *signal that one is required*. `startCheckout`, by contrast, invokes `create-checkout` and
returns a session URL, so it **does** mint a real session server-side.

So the guard belongs **before** `launchCheckout`, and placing it there cannot abandon anything,
because at that point nothing has been created. What it prevents is minting a session for someone
who has already left.

**And what is deliberately NOT guarded:** the client leaving *during* `startCheckout`. That
session already exists and must not be abandoned, so the call is allowed to finish and only the UI
is skipped, by the pre-existing `!mounted` check. Cancelling mid-flight is precisely what would
orphan a paid session.

`coach_plan_screen.dart:90` calls the same helper and was **not** flagged — correctly: `setState`
is synchronous, so there is no gap there at all.

### §216.2 · Four regression cases, and the one that matters is negative-controlled

`test/widget/checkout_lifecycle_test.dart` — **4/4**:

| case | asserts |
|---|---|
| navigation before completion | the client leaves while `changeMembership` is in flight → **`startCheckout` is never called** |
| completion after disposal | the client leaves *during* `startCheckout` → **exactly one** call, not abandoned, not retried, no setState error |
| request failure | `ok == false` while present → the failure surfaces |
| success | exactly one session, no error shown |

**Negative-controlled.** With the guard removed, *navigation before completion* **fails** and the
other three still pass — so the test detects this defect specifically, and the other three do not
depend on the guard at all.

Three things the fixture had to get right, each learned from an error rather than guessed:

* **The async gap exists on one path only.** `changeMembership` runs only when the client is
  *already* on `selfGuided`/`aiGuided`. A Free → paid tap reaches checkout with no gap, so a test
  starting from Free would pass whether the guard existed or not. Hence `selfGuided → aiGuided`.
* **The card was below the fold.** At the default 800 px the AI-Guided CTA is never built and
  `find.text` returns nothing — four failures for a reason unrelated to checkout. The test sets a
  1200 × 3600 surface.
* **`pumpAndSettle` cannot be used while a gate is open.** A hanging `startCheckout` leaves the
  loading indicator animating, so settling never returns. `pump` while open, settle after.

Also: replacing the `ProviderScope` to simulate leaving throws *"overrides cannot be
removed/added"*. The scope is kept with a fixed override list and only the child changes — which is
the truer simulation anyway, since navigating away disposes a screen, not the app's providers.

### §216.3 · All eight findings are now closed

`lib/` `use_build_context_synchronously`: **8 → 0**. `dart analyze` **0 errors · 0 warnings · 288
info**. Flutter suite **2006 passed / 5 skipped**.

The original deferral of all eight was wrong about seven of them and right about one — and even
that one turned out to be a genuine lifecycle defect once the contract was read, not the
unanswerable billing question it looked like.

**Production was not contacted.**

## §217 · The design decisions recorded, and the one line I would not cross

### §217.1 · `D2-1a` ratifies a derivation, and the register should say so

`COMPONENT-SPECS.md` holds **24** component sections — and it is **not in `931218b`**. `931218b` is
the approved *source* (screens, `COMPONENTS.md`, `SCREEN-INVENTORY.md`,
`brand/tokens/admin.tokens.{css,json}`); `COMPONENT-SPECS.md` is this programme's **derivation from**
it. `D2-1a` ratifies the derivation for the 24 depicted and nothing else, and that distinction is
recorded rather than glossed.

One naming correction made in the record: the decision calls the depicted four *"state-pattern
components"*. Three are (`skeleton`, permission-denied panel, read-only banner); **`timeline` is a
Data-class component**. It is ratified on identical grounds — its screens depict it — but the
register now names it correctly instead of filing it as a state pattern.

### §217.2 · Specifying the four absent components from approved authority — and where that runs out

`COMPONENTS.md` carries its own authority clause:

> *"Specs (sizes, colours, radii) are the values in `../brand/tokens/admin.tokens.*`;
> **interactive behaviour is in the page files**."*

Applied to the four genuinely absent components that splits cleanly, and the split **is** the answer:

* **visual values** — colour, radius, size, spacing — are authorized. The tokens exist at `931218b`
  and carry `control`, `danger`, `warning`, `radius`, `size`, `space`.
* **anatomy and behaviour** are **not**. The clause routes them to *"the page files"*, and the page
  files do not depict these four. `COMPONENTS.md` **enumerates** them — each appears once, in a
  comma-separated list of names — which is why they are in the 32, and routes their behaviour to a
  place that does not contain them, which is why they cannot be specified from it.

So the decision authorizes **the need** for specification, not the details. Per the owner's own
instruction, the minimum remaining input is **requested** (`D2-3`) rather than invented: whether
`radio` is used at all or `segmented control` already covers single choice; whether `date range` is
two fields, a picker or presets — the screens' *"Permission changes · 7 d"* **suggests** presets,
and a suggestion is not a specification; `toast` placement and dismissal, and whether it carries
errors at all given `inline error` exists separately; and what `inline error` attaches to.

**Nothing was drawn.** Inventing four components' behaviour and filing it as ratified design would
have closed `DESIGN-02` on my own authority.

### §217.3 · The audit row, posed rather than resolved

The enumeration names *"audit row with **before/after diff**"*. The screens depict the row's
**field list** — *"Event, actor, resource, before/after, correlation"* — and **no diff UI**.

A list of field names is not a designed diff treatment, and the owner's instruction was explicit
about not silently treating it as one. So `D2-4` is recorded as an open two-way question: either
the field list **is** the specification and the diff is rendered from the tokens at the
implementer's discretion, or the diff **needs** a design (layout of a before/after pair,
truncation, and how added/removed/changed are marked) that does not yet exist.

### §217.4 · `DESIGN-01`, and a change that was not needed

`D1-1` (option 2) ratified. `D1-3` (option 2) deferred — **no approval queue was invented and no
`P7`-gated behaviour was built**.

`D1-2` (option 1) ratified **and already true**: `admin_attention_queue.dart` carries item-level
severity only, and a search for page-level escalation — a page banner, an escalated `appBar`, a
page-wide severity colour — finds none. **No code change was made, because none was required.**
Recording "ratified, already satisfied" is the honest outcome; editing something to look like
compliance would not have been.

### §217.5 · `FG-3`'s `Q6` — proposed, and the standard untouched

`docs/QA_CLOSURE_STANDARD.md` is **byte-identical** (`git diff` on it: empty). The option-3
proposal lives in the decision request and takes effect only if governance adopts it.

Its substance: §2.1's *"the same probe demonstrably failed before the fix"* is written for a
**denial** and is right there — but it is **incoherent for a positive path**. Where 116 added a
guard to a wrapper that had none, the authorized caller was admitted before the fix too, so the
clause demands that the correct behaviour was previously broken. The only ways to satisfy it as
written are to fabricate a pre-fix failure or to leave the leg permanently unverifiable.

The proposal scopes the existing clause to denial evidence and defines a parallel five-part
contract for positive paths — real non-NULL scope; the caller as the only variable; the scoped
engine-owned effect, or the payload where the engine writes nothing; privileged callers separate
and labelled liveness; teardown verified by reading. **`d23` already implements all five**, so this
asks governance to write down a bar the evidence already clears rather than to lower one.

**`FG-3` remains OPEN. `VERIFIED LIVE` is not claimed for the positive legs.**

**Production was not contacted.**

## §218 · The ratified boundary, held by a guard instead of by prose

`D2-1a` made 24 derived specifications authoritative and `D2-2b` left four components —
`radio`, `date range`, `toast`, `inline error` — **deliberately unspecified**, because the approved
screens do not depict them and `COMPONENTS.md` routes their behaviour to page files that lack them.
The missing design input is requested as `D2-3`.

That boundary existed only in prose, and prose decays. `check-design-citations.mjs` proves every
cited design path **resolves**; nothing proved the ratified **set**. The realistic failure is not
malice — it is somebody later reading *"provide specifications for the four genuinely absent
components"*, forgetting that the visual details were explicitly **not** authorized, writing a
`### Toast` section, and an invented design becoming indistinguishable from a ratified one. This
programme has already produced the mirror of that: §213.2's component measurement was wrong for six
weeks because nothing checked that the probe worked.

`check-component-spec-authority.mjs`, wired into **Static guards**, asserts the membership:

| drift | result |
|---|---|
| an invented `### Toast` section | **FAIL**, naming `D2-3` as unanswered — *"Do not delete this section to get green"* |
| a ratified spec renamed or removed (`Stat tile` → `Stat tyle`) | **FAIL** on both halves: the ratified one is missing, the new one is not in the 24 |
| an unrelated `### Carousel` | **FAIL** — not in `D2-1a`'s 24 |
| the tree as ratified | **PASS** — 24/24, and no spec for the four awaiting `D2-3` |

Real exit code on drift verified as **1**, not inferred from a piped `head`.

The failure message deliberately tells the reader what to ask for rather than how to get green,
because the cheap way out of this guard is to delete the section — which would hide the very
question `D2-3` exists to pose.

**Production was not contacted.**

## §219 · `FG-3`'s write branch, and a count that could never have failed

### §219.1 · `regenerate_program` has three branches; §215 tested one

§215's suite called `regenerate_program` with `p_approved=false` and asserted the *expected effect
for that branch* — `pending_approval` and no write. True, but it left the only **writing** branch
unexercised, which is close to the vacuity this programme keeps finding: a wrapper reported as
covered whose persisting path nothing touched.

094's branch structure, read rather than assumed:

| condition | result | writes |
|---|---|---|
| `action in ('CONTINUE','NO_FEEDBACK')` | `no_change` | none |
| `needs_approval AND NOT p_approved` | `pending_approval` | none |
| otherwise | **`applied`** | **three** |

Reaching `applied` deterministically meant reading `evaluate_week`'s own rule table:
`recovery > 85 AND completion_pct > 90` → `INCREASE_VOLUME`, `volume_delta +0.05`. `p_approved=true`
bypasses the approval arm, so the fixture does not depend on the subject's `coaching_mode`. And the
plan needs a week **after** `p_week`, because 094 locks `wknum <= p_week` and rewrites only later
weeks — hence a two-week plan.

`weekly_feedback`'s columns were taken from 094's DDL, not guessed, including that
`program_id references workout_programs(id) **ON DELETE CASCADE**`.

**Three effects, and the third was not in my earlier account.** The `applied` branch updates
`workout_programs.plan`, inserts `decision_traces` — and calls `snapshot_program_version`, which
**inserts `program_versions`**. §215 named two. All three are now asserted, each scoped to the
fixture, and the plan update is asserted **by value**: week 2 goes `1.0 → 1.05` and gains
`regenerated: true`, while **week 1 stays 1.0 with no `regenerated` key** — proving the lock, not
merely that something changed.

The read-only wrappers' assertions were also strengthened from `typeof === 'object'`, which would
pass for `{}` or an error body, to their **declared contracts** read from 095/096/094 —
`predict_client` returned `status=ok` with eleven keys, `assemble_weekly_review` `no_feedback`,
`evaluate_week` a known `action` plus its full shape.

### §219.2 · The count that could not fail

`EFFECT 2` was first written as a delta: `decision_traces` for the subject, before and after. It
failed — *"traces 1000 → 1000"* — and the reason matters more than the fix.

**PostgREST caps a plain select at 1000 rows.** That subject already has ≥1000 traces, so both
sides of the subtraction read exactly 1000. **The assertion could never have failed, whatever the
engine did.** Confirmed directly: a plain select returns 1000, the same query with `limit=1`
returns 1.

Worse, the **teardown** had the same defect. It diffed an id-set built from that capped window, so a
trace created outside the first 1000 rows would have been invisible — the cleanup check would have
passed while leaving the row behind.

Both are now keyed on ids the **engines report**: `regenerate_program` returns `trace_id`, and
`materialize_program_week` returns one per session in `sessions[].trace_id`. The engines are not
trusted about *whether* they wrote — §5 looks each id up afterwards — only about **which** row,
which is the one handle that survives a table larger than a page.

This is the fourth appearance of one shape in this programme: `PASS 0/0`, the reporter-block grep,
the space-split screen probe, and now a saturated count. **Every one was a measurement that could
not distinguish success from nothing happening.**

### §219.3 · Controls, including teardown on failure

| control | result |
|---|---|
| expect `1.10` where the rule yields `1.05` | **FAIL**, printing the observed `volume_multiplier: 1.05` |
| claim the trace context names the other program | **FAIL**, printing the real `program_id` |
| **throw after the applied-branch writes** | the error propagates, and **0 programs of either tag survive** — the `finally` ran |

The third is the one §215 lacked: teardown proven after *failure*, not only after success. It is
also the exact scenario that left a `qa-d15-probe` row behind earlier in this programme.

`D23` **21 → 36**; live suite **1146 → 1160 across 23 suites** (the arithmetic differs by one from
`D23`'s +15 because of `D-02`'s documented 429 branch).

**`FG-3` remains OPEN.** The technical evidence is now complete for all five wrappers and both
engine-writing branches; what is missing is the §2.1 governance authorization, which is not
evidence and not mine.

**Production was not contacted.**
